column4: ### Genesis: The God Who Dwells With His Creation
column5: ### Genesis：The God who dwells with His creation

column4: A central theme in the narrative of God is His **desire to dwell** with His creation. This is clear in the stories throughout Genesis. Across its fifty chapters and genealogies from Adam (the first man) through Joseph (that last major figure in the book of Genesis, the last significant leader of God’s people before Moses), there is a period of approximately ~2,400 years. We can see through these stories the consistency of God’s goodness despite man’s wickedness.
column5: Within the narrative about God，一个核心主题是祂渴望与祂的受造物同住。This is clear throughout the story of Genesis。Spanning its fifty chapters，and from Adam（the first human）to Joseph（the last significant figure in Genesis、the last important leader among God's people before Moses）in the genealogies，the time span is approximately ~2,400 years。Through these stories，we can see that even when humanity is evil，God's goodness remains constant。

column4: In Genesis, God establishes relationship with select individuals.
column5: In Genesis，God establishes relationships with several specific individuals。

column4: 1.  **Adam and Eve** - The first humans, created by God and placed in the Garden of Eden. God walks and talks with them, giving them instructions and establishing a relationship of mutual love and obedience. However, this relationship is impacted by their disobedience in eating from the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil (Genesis 1-3).
column5: 1.  **Adam and Eve** - The first humans，created by God and placed in the Garden of Eden。God walked with them and spoke to them，giving them instructions and establishing a relationship of mutual love and obedience。However，this relationship was affected when they ate from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil（Genesis 1-3）。

column4: 2.  **Cain** - Although Cain ultimately rebels by murdering his brother Abel, God speaks directly to him, warning him about the danger of sin and offering him guidance before the murder. Even after Cain’s punishment, God marks him to protect him from harm (Genesis 4).
column5: 2.  **Cain** - Although Cain ultimately rebelled by murdering his brother Abel，God still spoke directly to him，warning him about the danger of sin and giving guidance before the murder occurred。Even after administering punishment to Cain，God set a mark on him to protect him from harm（Genesis 4）。

column4: 3.  **Noah** - God establishes a unique relationship with Noah, a righteous man, in a time of widespread corruption. God commands Noah to build an ark to save his family and the animals from the Flood. Afterward, God makes a covenant with Noah, promising never again to destroy the earth with a flood and establishing the rainbow as a sign of this covenant (Genesis 6-9).
column5: 3.  **Noah** - In an age of widespread corruption，God formed a unique relationship with Noah，a righteous man。God instructed Noah to build an ark to save his family and the animals from the flood。Afterward，God made a covenant with Noah，promising never again to destroy the earth with a flood，and gave the rainbow as the sign of this covenant（Genesis 6-9）。

column4: 4.  **Abraham (Abram)** - One of the most significant relationships in Genesis, God calls Abram to leave his homeland and promises to make him the father of a great nation. God establishes a covenant with Abram, promising land, descendants, and blessings for all nations through him. Abram’s faith and obedience become central themes, and his name is changed to Abraham as part of the covenant (Genesis 12, 15, 17, 22).
column5: 4.  **Abraham (Abram)** - One of the most important relationships in Genesis，God called Abram to leave his homeland and promised to make him the father of a great nation。God made a covenant with Abram，promising land、descendants、and to bless all nations through him。Abram's faith and obedience became central themes，and as part of the covenant his name was changed to Abraham（Genesis 12, 15, 17, 22）。

column4: 5.  **Hagar** - An Egyptian servant of Sarah, Hagar encounters God in the wilderness after being mistreated. God comforts her, promises her a future for her son Ishmael, and instructs her to return to Abraham and Sarah. Hagar refers to God as “El Roi” (“The God Who Sees Me”), recognizing His care for her (Genesis 16).
column5: 5.  **Hagar** - Sarah's Egyptian maidservant，who met God in the wilderness after being mistreated。God comforted her，promised a future for her son Ishmael，and instructed her to return to Abraham and Sarah。Hagar called God “El Roi”（“the God who sees me”），acknowledging His care for her（Genesis 16）。

column4: 6.  **Isaac** - The son of Abraham and Sarah, Isaac inherits the covenant promises made to his father. God reaffirms these promises directly to Isaac, including the promise of descendants and blessings. God also guides Isaac during a famine, protecting him and establishing the covenant relationship (Genesis 26).
column5: 6.  **Isaac** - The son of Abraham and Sarah，Isaac inherited the promises of the covenant God had made with his father。God reaffirmed these promises directly to Isaac，including the promise of descendants and blessing。God also guided and protected Isaac during a famine，establishing a covenant relationship（Genesis 26）。

column4: 7.  **Rebekah** - Although her relationship with God is indirect, God answers Rebekah’s prayer about her difficult pregnancy, revealing that her twins, Jacob and Esau, will become two nations with distinct destinies (Genesis 25).
column5: 7.  **Rebekah** - Although her relationship with God was more indirect，God still answered Rebekah's prayer about her difficult pregnancy，revealing that her twins，Jacob and Esau，would become two nations with different destinies（Genesis 25）。

column4: 8.  **Jacob** - God establishes a personal relationship with Jacob, appearing to him in a dream and confirming the covenant promises of land, descendants, and blessings. Jacob encounters God several times, including the famous wrestling match where God changes his name to Israel, symbolizing his transformation and the establishment of Israel as a people (Genesis 28, 32, 35).
column5: 8.  **Jacob** - God established a personal relationship with Jacob, appeared to him in dreams, and confirmed the covenantal promises concerning land, offspring, and blessing. Jacob encountered God multiple times, including the famous wrestling match during which God changed his name to Israel, symbolizing his transformation and the establishment of Israel as a nation (Genesis 28, 32, 35).

column4: 9.  **Joseph** - Although Joseph’s relationship with God isn’t based on direct appearances or covenants like those of Abraham or Jacob, God is deeply involved in his life. Through dreams, divine favor, and providence, God guides Joseph’s journey from being sold into slavery to becoming a powerful leader in Egypt. Joseph’s faith in God’s sovereignty allows him to forgive his brothers, recognizing that God used his suffering for good (Genesis 37, 39-50).
column5: 9.  **Joseph** - Although Joseph’s relationship with God was not based on direct manifestations or covenant-making like that of Abraham or Jacob, God was still deeply involved in his life. Through dreams, divine favor, and providence, God guided Joseph from being sold into slavery to becoming a powerful leader in Egypt. Joseph’s faith in God’s sovereignty enabled him to forgive his brothers, recognizing that God used his suffering to accomplish good (Genesis 37, 39-50).

column4: ### Exodus: The God Who Dwells With His People
column5: ### Exodus: The God Who Dwells with His People

column4: God’s desire to dwell with His people is also clearly seen in the second book of the Bible, Exodus. In the book of the exodus the people of Israel, who had lived for a period of time in relative peace and harmony in Egypt, are now being oppressed by a Pharaoh who did not know of Joseph and feared the Hebrews (Exodus 1:6-8). God’s people lived in Egypt for roughly ~400 years (Exodus 12:40-41), of which the later portion of that was spent living as slaves (there is not a universal consensus on precisely how long Israel was in bondage to Egypt).
column5: God’s desire to dwell with His people is also clearly revealed in the second book of the Bible, Exodus. In the book of Exodus, the Israelites, who had once lived in Egypt in relative peace and harmony for a time, were now oppressed by a Pharaoh who did not know Joseph and feared the Hebrews (Exodus 1:6-8). God’s people lived in Egypt for about ~400 years (Exodus 12:40-41), the latter half of which was spent in slavery (there is no universally agreed consensus regarding the exact length of Israel’s enslavement in Egypt).

column4: The phrase **“I AM THAT I AM”** (Ehyeh-Asher-Ehyeh) is one of the most profound self-revelations in Scripture. When Moses asks for God’s name, God responds with this phrase, which can be translated as "I Am Who I Am," "I Will Be Who I Will Be," or simply "I Am." This declaration on the surface is a bit confusing but holds deep meaning. Could you imagine introducing yourself to someone new as ‘I am’? When God reveals Himself as ‘I AM THAT I AM’ He is attesting to His nature, His eternal presence, His sovereignty. ‘I am’ is infinite in meaning and purpose.

This covenant (the Mosaic covenant) builds upon the Abrahamic covenant and lasts from Moses to Jesus.

column4: Despite building a covenant with His people, the relationship is one of a loving and jealous God pursuing and abiding with very stubborn and ungrateful people (Exodus 32:9). Ignoring God's miraculous intervention, they keep a rebellious attitude for large parts of the text. God even brings them to the promised land and tells them they can inherit it (Exodus 33:3), but in fear and disobedience they ignore the supernatural deliverance that God has given them, and instead must wander the desert for 40 years until almost everyone from that generation had died (Numbers 14:33-34).
column5: Despite God making a covenant with His people, this relationship is one in which a loving and jealous God pursues and dwells with a very stubborn and ungrateful people (Exodus 32:9). They disregarded God’s wondrous interventions and continued to rebel throughout much of the narrative. God even brought them to the Promised Land and told them they could receive it as an inheritance (Exodus 33:3), but out of fear and disobedience, they ignored God’s supernatural deliverance and instead had to wander in the wilderness for forty years, until almost that entire generation had died (Numbers 14:33-34).

column5: ### The Rest of the Old Testament

column4: In the ~1,400 years between the death of Moses and the birth of Christ the Israelites experienced a recurring cycle of devotion which brings God's favor and blessings, followed by rebellion, God’s judgment, their subsequent repentance, and ultimately God’s deliverance. This pattern is particularly evident in the books of **Judges, Kings, and Chronicles**, which recount cycles where the people turn away from God, often by worshiping other gods, resulting in periods of oppression or exile. In response to their cries, God repeatedly raised up judges, prophets, or leaders to deliver them.
column5: Over the ~1,400 years between Moses’ death and Christ’s birth, the Israelites repeatedly experienced a cycle: consecration brought God’s favor and blessing, followed by rebellion, God’s judgment, then repentance, and finally God’s deliverance. This pattern is especially evident in 《**Judges、Kings、Chronicles**》, which record the people turning away from God and often worshiping other gods, resulting in periods of oppression or exile. In response to their cries, God repeatedly raised up judges, prophets, or leaders to deliver them.

column4: Throughout these years, despite the Israelites' frequent failures to uphold their covenant with Him, God remains faithful, showing both justice and mercy. He continuously rescues and forgives His people, demonstrating His enduring commitment and love.
column5: During these years, despite the Israelites repeatedly failing and not keeping the covenant He made with them, God remained faithful, displaying both justice and mercy. He continually rescued and forgave His people, revealing His enduring commitment and love.

column4: God’s character and actions are fully expressed in the unity of Father, Son, and Spirit. The scriptures teach that God is one in essence, yet exists as three distinct persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Scripture affirms God’s oneness, stating, “beside Him there is no God” (Isaiah 45:5). However, the Godhead is understood as a **compound unity**-three distinct persons who cooperate with a singular mind and purpose, united in the truest sense. Each person of the Trinity has a unique role: the **Father creates**, the **Son redeems**, and the **Holy Spirit sanctifies**. The term “Trinity” does not appear in the Bible; it was developed as a theological expression to describe this concept, which is revealed through Scripture.
column5: God’s character and works are fully expressed in the unity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Scripture teaches that God is one in essence, yet exists as three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Scripture affirms God’s oneness, saying, “There is no God besides Me” (Isaiah 45:5). However, the Godhead is understood as a compound unity-three persons cooperating with the same mind and purpose, united as one in the truest sense. Each person of the Trinity has a distinct role: the Father creates, the Son redeems, and the Holy Spirit sanctifies. The term “Trinity” does not appear in Scripture; it is a theological term developed to describe this concept, which is revealed through the Bible.

column4: The Trinity can be illustrated by examples in nature, which help clarify this idea of unity in diversity. Like water, which can be liquid, ice, or vapor but remains H₂O, each person of the Trinity is fully God yet distinct in personhood. Or consider a triangle, with three sides and three angles, forming one complete shape; if one side is removed, it ceases to be a triangle. Similarly, **God’s nature is incomplete without all three persons**, who work together in perfect unity.
column5: The Trinity can be illustrated by examples from nature, which help clarify the idea of unity in diversity. For example, water can be liquid, ice, or vapor, yet it is still H₂O; each person of the Trinity is fully God, yet distinct in person. Or imagine a triangle, with three sides and three angles forming a complete shape; if one side is removed, it is no longer a triangle. Likewise, **if any person were missing, God’s nature would be incomplete**, and the three work together in perfect unity.

column4: - **God the Father**: He is the creator and sustainer of all things, often understood as the initiator in the Godhead. His love for humanity is central to the biblical story, exemplified in John 3:16. In our study we will examine God the father as the loving father and righteous judge, who made a path for our redemption.
column5: - **God the Father**: He is the Creator and Sustainer of all things, often understood as the initiator within the Godhead. His love for humanity is central to the biblical story, as shown in John 3:16. In our study, we will examine how God the Father, as the loving Father and righteous Judge, made a way for our redemption.

column4: - **God the Son**: Co-existent and co-eternal with the Father, Jesus took on human nature, being conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary. He lived a sinless life, died to redeem humanity, and rose again, defeating sin and death. He now sits at the Father’s right hand, interceding for us (John 1:1-3; Matthew 1:23; 1 Timothy 2:5). In our study we will examine Jesus as the perfect atoning sacrifice, the resurrected Lord, and head of the church.
column5: - **The Son**: Jesus, coexistent and coeternal with the Father, took on human nature, was conceived by the Holy Spirit, and born of the virgin Mary. He lived a sinless life, died to redeem humanity, and rose again, conquering sin and death. He now sits at the right hand of the Father, interceding for us (John 1:1-3；Matthew 1:23；1 Timothy 2:5). In our study, we will examine Jesus as the perfect atoning sacrifice, the risen Lord, and the head of the church.

column4: - **God the Holy Spirit**: The Holy Spirit, co-existent and equal with the Father and the Son, is sent by the Father through the Son to convict the world of sin and prepare believers as the Bride of Christ. He empowers, comforts, and sanctifies those who are in Christ (John 14:26; 15:26; 16:8). In our study we will examine the Holy Spirit as the comforter, given to us by God to equip, empower, sanctify, and abide with us.
column5: - **The Holy Spirit**: The Holy Spirit is coexistent and coequal with the Father and the Son, sent by the Father through the Son to convict the world of sin and to prepare believers as the Bride of Christ. He gives power, comfort, and sanctifies those who are in Christ (John 14:26；15:26；16:8). In our study, we will examine the Holy Spirit as the Helper, whom God gives to equip, empower, sanctify, and be with us.

column4: Through these distinct persons, God’s triune nature is revealed as a perfect union in purpose, will, and love, each person playing a vital role in the divine mission of creation, redemption, and sanctification. The Trinity invites believers to experience God fully, both as a loving Father, a redeeming Savior, and a transforming Spirit.
column5: Through the persons of these three, God’s triune nature is manifested as perfect unity in purpose, will, and love; in the divine mission of creation, redemption, and sanctification, each plays a vital role. The Trinity invites believers to experience God fully: as the loving Father, the redeeming Savior, and the Spirit who transforms hearts.

column5: ## Conclusion

column4: We can be uniquely known by our names: husband, father, son, brother, friend. Each of these a declaration of who we are in relation to someone else. We can also be known by our attributes: faithful, patient, kind, intelligent, funny. Likewise, we can know God by His attributes and names- He is our Healer, Provider, Shepherd, and Redeemer. However, as labels and words are only a small part of us, for ourselves to be truly known by others, we must be experienced. Even more so with God. To truly and fully know Him we must experience Him.
column5: We can be uniquely known by names: husband, father, son, brother, friend. Each is a declaration of our identity in relationship to others. We can also be known by attributes: faithful, patient, kind, wise, humorous. Likewise, we can know God through His attributes and names- He is our Healer, Provider, Shepherd, and Redeemer. Yet titles and words are only a small part of us; for others to truly know us, we must be actually experienced. This is even more true of God. To truly and fully know Him, we must experience Him.

column4: God’s names reveal His character, but personal encounters deepen our understanding of what these names signify. For instance, “God my Healer” takes on a richer, more profound meaning when we understand the depths of illness, desperation, or helplessness from which God rescues. Knowing Him as our Provider is transformed when we have felt true need and found Him faithful.
column5: God’s names reveal His character, but personal encounters deepen our understanding of what those names mean. For example, “the God who heals me” takes on richer, deeper meaning when we understand that God has rescued us from the depths of sickness, despair, or helplessness. Knowing Him as our Provider is also transformed when we face real need and find Him faithful.

column4: Scriptures offer a context to these encounters, showing us God’s faithfulness to His people across time and circumstance, reinforcing how His names and attributes are not mere titles but realities He brings to life, experienced in the lives of individuals. It is through this interplay of personal experience and the scriptural narrative that we come to know God-not just as a distant description but as a present, active relationship in every season of our lives.
column5: The Bible provides the context for these encounters, showing us God’s faithfulness to His people across time and circumstances, reinforcing the fact that His names and attributes are not merely titles but realities He brings to life and that are experienced in people’s lives. It is through the interplay of personal experience and the biblical narrative that we come to know God-not merely as a distant description, but as a relationship present with us and actively at work in every season of our lives.
